extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of poetry; practicing critics and readers learning practical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reading and evaluating poems by identifying misreadings (stock responses, sentimentality, impersonality) and by applying internal, experience-grounded standards rather than external comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: No poem can be judged by standards external to itself
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic should not judge a poem by standards that belong to other poems or to outside conventions; poems must be read on their own terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards: 'intelligent critics, however, who realise that no poem can be judged by standards external to itself, have no excuse.' Use internal evidence of the poem rather than comparing it to a 'stock' model; comparisons may be used only to bring out features, not as external yardsticks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware stock responses that distort reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Stock responses—standardised, familiar reactions—can intervene and distort a passage or replace the poem's particular meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited (e.g., 3.15, 5.37, 5.38, 5.4, 8.3–8.33, 13.1–13.4) where stock sentiments replace the poem and bring it into discredit. Critics should notice when a reader's response is an automatic stock reaction rather than a careful engagement with the poem's particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise when stock responses are native to the poem (facility/impersonality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the poem itself invokes only stock responses throughout its items and cadences; native familiarity and impersonality are signs of composition from stock responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators: extreme impersonality, absence of personal twist in phrasing or movement, 'might well have been written by a committee.' Compare with poems that show individual character (Donne's Sonnet). Such native facility suggests the poem is composed of stock responses and merits scrutiny on that basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish native familiarity from acquired familiarity (ability to surprise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Familiarity that is 'native'—present on first reading and unavoidable—differs from that acquired by repeated readings; native familiarity indicates stock patterning and lacks the capacity to surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast: Hamlet's soliloquy can still surprise on re-reading (acquired familiarity), whereas stock poems possess a familiarity that belongs to them at first reading and signals limited imaginative movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge responses by two tests: appropriateness to situation and obstruction of further responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses should be evaluated both for how appropriate they are to the situation the poem presents and for the degree to which they prevent more appropriate, refined responses from developing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards: these are 'partially independent sets of considerations.' Some stock responses are admirable and adequate; others are inappropriate and powerful enemies to poetry. Apply both tests when assessing a reader's reaction or a poem's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not take expected stock responses for granted
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem that seems to 'draw out' a stock response but in reality does not genuinely move the reader should not be credited merely because an expected reaction was anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: correspondent's reading of Gray's Elegy vs Poem 13 — one may expect certain feelings but only on rereading discover that the poem failed to touch deeply; critics must check whether the response was genuinely elicited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider sources of ideas: experience, suggestion, intellectual elaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas (and attached emotional responses) come from direct experience, suggestion from others, and our own intellectual elaboration; each source has different reliability for poetic understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestion and elaboration are indispensable (necessary for rapid acquisition of ideas) but also dangerous; much transmitted material (cinema, press, teachers) is crude by poetic standards. Be cautious of ideas acquired parasitically rather than from lived experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: See withdrawal from experience as a chief cause of stereotyped reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Withdrawal—physical, moral, conventional, or intellectual—tends to fix inappropriate, stereotyped responses that misread poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes listed: lack of exposure (e.g., city child never seeing sea), moral deprivation, excessive inculcation, or theorising that hides reality. Corrective: closer contact with reality and broader, available experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat ideas as imperfect representations coloured by subjective feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'idea' is less than a full replica of its object (a sketch that distorts) and more than a replica because it includes the subject's interest and feelings; this colouring affects reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that our mental representation reflects needs, desires, habits and may bias interpretation. Use this awareness to test whether a reader's response springs from the poem or from pre-existing ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use closer contact with reality (experience/other minds) as corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: The main corrective to inappropriate or stock responses is closer contact with reality—either direct experience or mediated through minds closer to reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards: poetry itself can be a tool to break up unreal ideas, but bad poetry can reinforce them. Encourage reading that reorganises the reader's responses rather than confirming what they already feel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'sentimental' quantitatively: emotions too easily stirred
rubrics_metrics.description: One sense of 'sentimental' is quantitative — a person or response is sentimental if emotions are too readily or too strongly triggered for the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Touchiness varies with circumstances (drugs, weather, fatigue, music, crowds, illness). To judge sentimentality in this sense, take careful account of the situation and possible extraneous facilitators of emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'sentimental' qualitatively: crude versus refined emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Another sense of 'sentimental' is qualitative — crude emotions are broadly arousable by many situations, while refined emotions require a narrow range of situations; crude ≠ intense, refined ≠ weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refined responses are more capable of appropriateness but more liable to error; crude responses are less likely to hit delicate truth. Note that intensity (violence of emotion) is not the same as poetic value—the 'depth, not the tumult, of the soul' matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat 'sentiment' as a persisting organised disposition that can become inappropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentiment is not a momentary experience but a relatively permanent set of tendencies and dispositions formed by past experience; such sentiments may persist and become mismatched to present reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: continued deference to an old schoolmaster, veterans' changing sentiments about war. Critics should note when sentiments invoked by a poem are outdated or inappropriate to current conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague abuse—be precise when accusing sentimentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling something 'sentimental' as a vague insult is unhelpful; critics should aim for precise, testable statements rather than foggy abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards compares vague accusation to aiming with putty; precise criticism (like a bullet) may miss but is more useful for diagnosing what is wrong. Where possible specify whether the fault is excessive intensity, crudeness, inappropriateness to occasion, or persistence of outdated sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise that good poetry often disconcerts habitual responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Great poetry tends to disturb familiar habits of feeling and thought; the capacity to disconcert habitual stock responses is a sign of poetic power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards: 'Nearly all good poetry is disconcerting, for a moment at least.' This overturning of habits may temporarily bewilder but is an indicator that the poem fosters reorganisation of the reader's responses; treat such disconcertion as a potential merit rather than a flaw.
